Q133132.title: Paris Commune
paras: The Paris Commune was the revolutionary government that held Paris for 72 days, from 18 March to 28 May 1871, in defiance of the French national government of Adolphe Thiers, which sat at Versailles. Its supporters, the Communards, were mostly Parisian workers and artisans organised in the city's National Guard, some 180,000 strong, led by republicans, Jacobins, Blanquists, followers of Proudhon and members of the First International. Against them stood the National Assembly elected in February 1871, which had a monarchist majority, and the regular army.

The revolt grew out of France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. Paris had held out through a four-month German siege and resented the armistice signed by Jules Favre with Bismarck in January 1871 and the peace terms Thiers accepted, including a German victory parade on the Champs-Élysées on 1 March. The new Assembly, mainly provincial and monarchist, moved from Bordeaux to Versailles rather than Paris, ended the National Guard's pay and the wartime moratorium on rents and debts, which threatened many Parisians with ruin.

On the night of 17–18 March Thiers sent troops to take back the cannons, 227 by the City of Paris's count, that the National Guard had moved to Montmartre and Belleville. Crowds, many of them women, and guardsmen surrounded the soldiers, who fraternised with them; generals Lecomte and Thomas were shot. The attempt to disarm Paris had failed, and the insurrection had begun. Elections on 26 March produced the Commune's council. Divided between a Jacobin majority and a socialist minority, it introduced measures including secular education, the separation of church and state and steps towards equal pay for women, but it did not take the offensive against Versailles. Short-lived communes in Lyon, Marseille, Saint-Étienne and other towns were quickly suppressed.

Thiers's army, now much stronger, entered Paris and during the 'Bloody Week' of 21–28 May crushed the Commune; many Communards were shot after surrendering. The number killed is uncertain: Wikipedia cites estimates of 10,000 to 15,000, the City of Paris gives about 20,000, and scholars cited by EBSCO put it as high as 30,000. Karl Marx wrote a defence of the Commune soon after its fall, and its memory has remained powerful in France and abroad.

Q153858.title: Battle of Tannenberg (1914)
paras: The Battle of Tannenberg was fought in East Prussia in the last days of August 1914, at the start of the First World War, between the German Eighth Army, commanded by Paul von Hindenburg with Erich Ludendorff as his chief of staff, and the Russian Second Army of General Aleksandr Samsonov. It ended with the encirclement and destruction of most of Samsonov's army, the most complete German victory of the war.

Russia invaded East Prussia sooner than Germany expected, with two armies: the First Army under Pavel Rennenkampf from the east and Samsonov's Second Army from the south, intended to trap the outnumbered Germans between them. After Rennenkampf beat the Germans at Gumbinnen on 20 August, the German commander Maximilian von Prittwitz proposed abandoning East Prussia and was replaced by Hindenburg and Ludendorff. They adopted a plan prepared by Prittwitz's operations officer Max Hoffmann: leaving only a cavalry screen facing Rennenkampf, who had paused, they moved almost the whole army south against Samsonov, part of it by rail.

The Russian armies were poorly coordinated, and many of their radio messages were sent uncoded, so the Germans could read their plans; Samsonov advanced without knowing either the German strength or that Rennenkampf had halted. From 26 August German corps under Hermann von François and August von Mackensen attacked both of Samsonov's flanks, and by 29 August they had closed the ring around the Russian centre. Samsonov ordered a retreat too late and, after the defeat, is believed to have taken his own life.

Russian losses were enormous, though figures differ: History Hit gives about 95,000 captured and 78,000 killed or wounded out of some 150,000 men, while EBSCO gives 122,000 prisoners and 500 guns, against German losses of about 15,000. Hindenburg and Ludendorff became national heroes, and the battle was named after the medieval Tannenberg (Grunwald), where the Teutonic Knights had been defeated in 1410, about 30 km away. The Russian invasion had nonetheless made Germany move troops east, which may have helped the French at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914.

Q152120.title: Wannsee Conference
paras: On 20 January 1942, at noon, Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Security Police and SD and of the Reich Security Main Office, held a meeting of about 90 minutes in an SS guesthouse, a villa on the Großer Wannsee lake in Berlin. Fifteen senior officials attended: state secretaries and other officials of Reich ministries, among them Josef Bühler of Hans Frank's General Government in occupied Poland, and representatives of the Nazi Party and the SS, including the Gestapo chief Heinrich Müller and Adolf Eichmann, who kept the minutes. The subject was the so-called 'Final Solution of the Jewish Question'.

The mass murder of Europe's Jews was already under way. It had begun with the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, where SS mobile units carried out mass shootings, killing more than 33,000 people at Babyn Yar near Kyiv in September 1941 alone, and from late 1941 gas vans were used; deportations from the Reich had started in October 1941. According to the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb), at least half a million people had been murdered by the time of the conference. In July 1941 Göring had commissioned Heydrich to prepare an overall plan for the 'Final Solution'.

Heydrich used the meeting to assert his leading role and to secure the cooperation of the ministries and party offices whose help he needed for deportations across Europe. The minutes, written by Eichmann in bureaucratic euphemism, counted some eleven million Jews, including those in countries Germany did not control such as Britain, Ireland, Sweden and Switzerland, who were to be 'evacuated to the East'. Those able to work would be used in labour columns building roads, where many would die, and any survivors would be 'treated accordingly'. The participants raised no objection; they offered proposals and discussed the fate of people of mixed descent and in mixed marriages, and Bühler asked that the General Government be dealt with first.

The decision to murder the Jews of Europe had been taken at a higher political level before the meeting, and the conference itself did not decide it. Its importance lies in the coordination that extended the genocide to almost the whole of Europe and in the complicity of the German state administration. Soon afterwards gas chambers were built at Auschwitz, where large transports of Jews began arriving in March 1942; by the war's end more than six million Jews had been murdered. A copy of the minutes was found in 1947 among German Foreign Office files, and since 1992 the villa has been a memorial and education centre.

Q253224.title: Armistice of 11 November 1918
paras: The armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War on the Western Front was signed at about 5 a.m. on 11 November 1918 in the railway carriage that served as Marshal Ferdinand Foch's office, on a siding in the forest of Compiègne, north of Paris. Foch, Supreme Commander of the Allied armies, and Admiral Rosslyn Wemyss, the British First Sea Lord, signed for the Allies. For Germany signed the Centre Party politician Matthias Erzberger, who led the delegation, the diplomat Count Alfred von Oberndorff, Major-General Detlof von Winterfeldt for the army command and Captain Ernst Vanselow of the navy. Hostilities stopped at 11 a.m. Paris time.

In November 1918 the chancellor, Prince Max of Baden, appointed Erzberger to the armistice commission, so that, unusually, politicians rather than soldiers led the talks. When the delegates met Foch, he made them state that they were asking for an armistice and then had the Allied conditions read out; the Germans were given 72 hours to reply and had little room to negotiate. Meanwhile revolution swept Germany: Prince Max was forced out, Emperor William II abdicated and a republic was proclaimed under a socialist provisional government led by Friedrich Ebert. On the evening of 10 November the new chancellor telegraphed his acceptance, and in a final session the Germans obtained only minor changes before signing.

The 34 articles were designed to leave Germany unable to resume the war. Germany had to evacuate Belgium, France, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine and withdraw from the left bank of the Rhine, which Allied armies would occupy; to hand over 5,000 guns, 25,000 machine guns, 1,700 aircraft, all its submarines, and to have designated surface warships disarmed and interned; to renounce the treaties of Brest-Litovsk and Bucharest; and to accept that the Allied blockade would continue. The armistice was set for 36 days and was extended three times, in December 1918, January and February 1919, until the Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919. Erzberger, who also urged acceptance of the Versailles treaty, was blamed by nationalists for the defeat and was assassinated in 1921.

Q150939.title: Operation Weserübung
paras: Operation Weserübung was Germany's surprise attack on neutral Denmark and Norway at dawn on 9 April 1940. Under General Nikolaus von Falkenhorst, German forces landed from warships at the main Norwegian ports from Oslo to Narvik and dropped paratroopers on the airfields at Fornebu near Oslo and Sola near Stavanger, while Denmark was attacked and occupied the same day. Norway resisted, under King Haakon VII and its government, with help from Britain and France; it was the first large operation in which German land, sea and air forces fought under a single command.

Both sides saw Norway's strategic value. Germany's arms industry depended on Swedish iron ore, which in winter was shipped from Narvik down the Norwegian coast, and Grand Admiral Erich Raeder wanted naval bases in Norway. The Allies planned to land at Narvik on the pretext of helping Finland in the Winter War and later to mine Norwegian waters to stop the ore traffic. After meeting the Norwegian Nazi Vidkun Quisling in December 1939, Hitler ordered a study of an invasion; the 'Altmark' incident in February 1940, when a British destroyer freed British prisoners from a German ship in Norwegian waters, sped up the planning. Britain began laying mines off Norway on 8 April, as the German fleets were already at sea.

Most Norwegian towns fell quickly on 9 April. But in the Oslofjord the old fortress of Oscarsborg opened fire on the heavy cruiser Blücher, which was carrying troops to take the capital, and sank it at 06:22. The delay let the king, the government and parliament escape from Oslo together with the national gold reserves, and they refused German demands to appoint Quisling as prime minister. Oslo was taken that day by troops flown in to Fornebu.

Allied troops landed around Narvik and at Åndalsnes and Namsos in mid-April, but they were too few and lacked air cover. Fighting in southern Norway ended around the turn of April and May. The Allies took Narvik on 28 May, but the German offensive in France forced them to withdraw; an Allied evacuation on 5–8 June took the king and government into exile in Britain, and Norwegian forces in the north surrendered on 10 June. Germany secured the ore route and bases for its navy and air force, but tied down a large occupation army, some 300,000 men according to EBSCO, until 1945. In Britain the failure of the campaign led to Chamberlain's replacement by Churchill.

Q242099.title: Mukden incident
paras: On the evening of 18 September 1931 an explosion damaged a section of the Japanese-owned South Manchuria Railway near the city of Mukden (Shenyang) in north-east China. Japan's Kwantung Army, stationed in Manchuria, blamed Chinese nationalists and used the incident as a pretext to invade the region. According to EBSCO the explosion was staged by the Kwantung Army itself; the U.S. Office of the Historian's account notes that it was suspected that mid-level Japanese officers had planted the bomb to provide a pretext.

Japan had long claimed 'special interests' in Manchuria, with its railways, ports and resources, and three years earlier the Kwantung Army had assassinated the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin. After 18 September its troops drove the Chinese forces out of the region, meeting little resistance, and by early 1932 they controlled all of Manchuria; the Japanese government could not rein them in. In March 1932 Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as its nominal head, while the real power lay with the Kwantung Army. Japanese forces also attacked Shanghai in 1932.

The League of Nations sent a commission under Lord Lytton, whose 1932 report found that Chinese territory had been seized by force and refused to recognise Manchukuo. The United States, under the Stimson Doctrine of early 1932, declared that it would not recognise agreements that violated its treaty rights. Neither had any effect. After the Japanese delegate Yōsuke Matsuoka made an impassioned speech against the report in Geneva on 24 February 1933, Japan announced its withdrawal from the League on 27 March 1933. Some historians have argued that the crisis marked the beginning of the Second World War.

Q153992.title: Reichstag fire
paras: On the night of 27 February 1933, four weeks after Adolf Hitler had been sworn in as Chancellor of Germany, the Reichstag building in Berlin, home of the German parliament, was set on fire. A Berlin fire station received the alarm shortly after 9 p.m.; by the time firefighters arrived the building was in flames, and much of it, including the main chamber, was gutted. Police found and arrested Marinus van der Lubbe, a young unemployed Dutchman with communist views, inside the building. He said he had acted alone, to rouse the workers against the state.

A new election had been called for 5 March. Hitler and Hermann Göring, the Prussian interior minister, at once declared the fire the signal for a communist uprising. The next day, at Hitler's request, President Paul von Hindenburg used the emergency powers of Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution to sign the Reichstag Fire Decree. It suspended freedom of speech, of the press and of assembly and the secrecy of post and telephone, and removed limits on police arrests. Thousands of communists, among them the party's leaders and Reichstag deputies, were imprisoned in the following days.

With the Communist Party crushed, the Nazis raised their share of the vote on 5 March from 33 to 44 per cent according to Wikipedia, and with their allies of the German National People's Party they held a majority. On 23 March the Reichstag, now meeting in the Kroll Opera House, passed the Enabling Act, which let Hitler's government make laws without parliament. The decree's suspension of civil rights was never lifted under Nazi rule.

Van der Lubbe was tried before the Reich Supreme Court in Leipzig from September to December 1933, together with the German communist Ernst Torgler and three Bulgarian Comintern members, among them Georgi Dimitrov. Only van der Lubbe was convicted; he was beheaded on 10 January 1934, and in 2008 Germany posthumously pardoned him. Who was behind the fire has been argued over ever since: communists at the time accused the Nazis of starting it themselves, and while most historians since the 1960s have accepted that van der Lubbe acted alone, some, such as Benjamin Hett in 2013, have argued that he cannot have done so.

Q204213.title: Romanian Revolution (1989)
paras: In 1989, while Poland, Hungary, East Germany and Czechoslovakia began to open up, Romania's communist dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu refused any reform. His regime rested on a personality cult and the Securitate secret police, and to pay off foreign debt it exported food while rationing food and energy at home. The spark came in the western city of Timișoara, where the authorities tried to move László Tőkés, a dissident pastor of the Hungarian Reformed Church, to a remote parish. His supporters blockaded his house on 15 December, and from 16 December the protest grew into a mass uprising joined by thousands of residents.

The army, the Securitate and the police opened fire; dozens were shot dead on 17 December, but the protests went on, factories and the university struck, and the army withdrew to its barracks. On 20 December Timișoara became the first Romanian city free of communist rule. On 21 December Ceaușescu spoke to a crowd of about 100,000 from the Central Committee building in Bucharest; the crowd turned against him, and fighting broke out that day in Bucharest and other cities.

On 22 December, with the building besieged by huge crowds, Ceaușescu and his wife Elena fled by helicopter from its roof and were arrested the same afternoon in the town of Târgoviște. Ion Iliescu, a former communist official, announced on television the formation of the National Salvation Front to take over the government. On 25 December a military tribunal sentenced the Ceaușescus to death in a summary trial, and they were shot at once.

More than 1,100 people were killed in the revolution, most of them after Ceaușescu's fall, in street fighting blamed at the time on unidentified 'terrorists' loyal to the old regime. The official figure cited by Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education is 1,165 dead; the organisers of the 2019 commemoration in Bucharest gave 1,142. Iliescu won the presidential election of May 1990, and whether December 1989 was a popular revolution or a coup by his circle is still disputed: in 2019 he was put on trial, accused of having stoked the bloodshed to legitimise his own power, which he denied.

Q208191.title: Asian–African Conference
paras: From 18 to 24 April 1955 representatives of 29 Asian and African governments met in Bandung, Indonesia, for the first large conference of its kind. Most of the participants had only recently won independence from colonial rule. The meeting was organised by Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Pakistan, which had agreed on it at a planning meeting in Bogor in December 1954; Indonesia's President Sukarno and India's Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru were among its leading figures, and the People's Republic of China sent its premier, Zhou Enlai.

The aims were to promote economic and cultural co-operation, to oppose colonialism and racism, and to give the new nations a voice in a world divided by the Cold War. The main debate was over whether Soviet rule in Eastern Europe and Central Asia should be condemned alongside Western colonialism; the delegates compromised by condemning 'colonialism in all of its manifestations'. Zhou Enlai, who had escaped an assassination attempt on his way to the meeting, struck a moderate, conciliatory tone that eased the fears of anti-communist delegates.

On 24 April the delegates adopted a final communiqué calling for economic and cultural co-operation, human rights and self-determination, an end to racial discrimination and peaceful coexistence. It included a ten-point declaration on world peace, building on the United Nations Charter and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence agreed between India and China in 1954, which stressed respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, the equality of races and nations, and non-interference in other countries' internal affairs.

The United States had watched the conference warily, fearing that it would turn against the West, but the participants held a wide range of views and no general denunciation of the West followed. Bandung showed that the newly independent states could act together in world politics, and its principles helped lay the foundations of the Non-Aligned Movement, although the 'spirit of Bandung' had faded by the end of the 1960s.

Q217981.title: Allied invasion of Sicily
paras: After Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in May 1943, the United States and Britain decided to keep up the pressure in the Mediterranean rather than wait for the invasion of France. Meeting at Casablanca, Allied leaders chose Sicily as the next target: taking it could knock Fascist Italy out of the war, secure the sea lanes of the central Mediterranean and draw German divisions away from other fronts. To hide the target, British intelligence carried out Operation Mincemeat, planting false invasion plans on a corpse washed ashore in Spain, which led Hitler to reinforce Sardinia and Corsica instead.

Operation Husky, under the overall command of General Dwight D. Eisenhower, began on the night of 9-10 July 1943. A storm scattered the American paratroopers and British glider troops, but the seaborne landings that followed at dawn, after heavy naval and air bombardment, succeeded. The U.S. Seventh Army under General George S. Patton came ashore on the left and the British Eighth Army under General Bernard Montgomery on the right, along the south-eastern coast of the island. The figures for the armada differ: the Oxford Companion to American Military History gives 2,500 ships and 180,000 men landed on the first day, HISTORY.com about 3,000 ships and 150,000 troops.

Italian defenders offered little resistance at first, but German armour counter-attacked the next morning and nearly drove the Americans back into the sea at Gela; within two days the beachheads were secure. Over the following weeks Montgomery pushed up the east coast while Patton swung north-west and then east along the north coast towards Messina. The invasion shook the Fascist regime: in late July 1943 Mussolini was deposed and arrested, and the new government under Marshal Pietro Badoglio began secret armistice talks with the Allies.

When American troops entered Messina on 17 August 1943 the campaign was over, but most of the German forces, with much of their equipment, had already escaped across the Strait of Messina to the mainland (HISTORY.com puts the number of Germans and Italians who crossed at 100,000). The capture of Sicily and its airfields opened the way for the Allied landings on the Italian mainland in September 1943.

Q219230.title: Marco Polo Bridge incident
paras: On the night of 7 July 1937 Japanese and Chinese troops clashed near the Marco Polo Bridge (Lugou Bridge), an old stone bridge by the small walled town of Wanping, about a dozen miles south-west of Beiping (Beijing). Japan's China Garrison Army was stationed in the area, and one of its companies was holding night exercises near the bridge, while Wanping was held by the Chinese 29th Army.

According to a study by Japan's National Institute for Defense Studies, based on Japanese and Chinese records, shots were heard from the Chinese side at about 22:40, and at roll call one Japanese private was found missing. The regimental commander, Colonel Mutaguchi, sent a battalion to demand an explanation at Wanping. The soldier soon turned up, but the case had already turned a shooting into a dispute. After more shots in the early hours the Japanese battalion advanced, the Chinese opened fire, and at dawn on 8 July both sides went into action.

Local commanders agreed a ceasefire on 11 July, and neither high command at first wanted a full war: in Tokyo a group around Major General Ishiwara Kanji tried to keep the fighting local. But mutual mistrust drove both sides on. Chiang Kai-shek ordered Wanping held at any cost and sent troops north, and the Japanese army leadership came to favour a decisive blow. Japan used the incident to seize the nearby railway and occupied Beiping and Tianjin by the end of July; in August the fighting spread to Shanghai, and by the end of the year the Chinese capital, Nanjing, had fallen.

The clash grew into the Second Sino-Japanese War, which lasted until 1945. To limit the risk of Western involvement Japan did not formally declare war until late 1941 and called the conflict the 'China Incident'. Although the Second World War is usually dated from September 1939, historians such as Christopher Reed argue that its roots reach back to this clash.

Q223732.title: Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel
paras: Britain governed Palestine under a mandate from the League of Nations that was due to end in May 1948. On 29 November 1947 the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, which proposed dividing the mandate into a Jewish state and an Arab state when British rule ended in May 1948, with Jerusalem and its surroundings under international administration. The Palestinian Arabs rejected the plan as unfair, and fighting broke out at once between Arab irregulars and the Jewish forces of the Haganah and the smaller Irgun and LEHI groups.

On 14 May 1948, the day the British Mandate ended, David Ben-Gurion, head of the Jewish Agency, proclaimed in Tel Aviv, at a session of the People's Council, 'the establishment of a Jewish State in Eretz-Israel, to be known as the State of Israel', with effect from the end of the mandate that night. The text based the claim on the Jewish people's historic bond with the land, the Balfour Declaration of 1917, the League of Nations mandate, the murder of millions of Jews in Europe and the UN resolution.

The declaration promised a state open to Jewish immigration, based on 'freedom, justice and peace' and guaranteeing equal social and political rights to all inhabitants regardless of religion, race or sex. It made the People's Council a provisional council of state until an elected constituent assembly adopted a constitution, appealed to the Arab inhabitants to take part in building the state as equal citizens, and offered peace to neighbouring states. U.S. President Harry S. Truman recognised the new state the same day, against the advice of his State Department.

War followed immediately. Arab aircraft attacked Tel Aviv, and the armies of Egypt, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq invaded the former mandate, with Transjordan's forces fighting in the areas assigned to the Arab state and in Jerusalem. Israeli forces went on to the offensive, and armistice agreements signed in 1949 left Israel with more territory than the UN plan had allotted it, while Egypt held the Gaza Strip and Jordan the West Bank.

Q2305266.title: Soviet invasion of Poland
paras: On 17 September 1939, sixteen days after Nazi Germany had invaded Poland from the west, the Soviet Red Army crossed Poland's eastern border. The attack followed from the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of August 1939, whose secret protocol had divided Poland between Germany and the Soviet Union. In the early hours the Polish ambassador in Moscow, Wacław Grzybowski, was handed a note justifying the attack; he refused to accept it. Moscow claimed that the Polish state had ceased to exist and that it was protecting the Ukrainians and Belarusians of eastern Poland.

The Polish army, already broken by the German offensive, was retreating east and south-east. Facing a second enemy, the commander-in-chief, Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły, ordered his troops not to fight the Red Army except in self-defence and to withdraw towards Romania and Hungary. Border guards and scattered units still resisted at places such as Grodno, Wilno (Vilnius) and Szack. According to Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), the Soviets committed more than 600,000 soldiers, 4,700 tanks and 3,300 aircraft. Where Soviet and German forces met, the Germans pulled back and handed over their Polish prisoners.

On 28 September Germany and the Soviet Union signed a treaty in Moscow fixing their new border. The Soviet Union took about three-fifths of Poland's territory and some 13 million of its people; the Vilnius region was handed to Lithuania, and the rest was annexed in November 1939 as 'Western Belarus' and 'Western Ukraine'.

Soviet troops shot prisoners from the start: the IPN cites historians' estimates of some 2,500 prisoners and several hundred civilians murdered in September 1939 alone. Nearly two years of occupation followed, with arrests, deportations to the interior of the Soviet Union and the Katyn massacre, until Germany attacked the Soviet Union in June 1941.

Q318161.title: Helsinki Accords
paras: The Helsinki Final Act was signed on 1 August 1975 in Helsinki, Finland, at the close of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE). Its 35 signatories were the United States, Canada and the states of Europe on both sides of the Cold War divide, including the Soviet Union, East and West Germany and the Holy See; only Albania, under Enver Hoxha, refused to take part (Wikipedia also lists tiny Andorra as absent).

The idea went back to the 1950s, when the Soviet Union first proposed a European security conference in the hope of winning formal recognition of the borders drawn in Eastern Europe after the Second World War. The West held back for years, but détente in the early 1970s changed its mind: preliminary consultations began in Helsinki in 1972, the conference opened in July 1973, and two years of negotiation, mostly in Geneva, followed before the leaders met in Helsinki for the signing.

The Act was a political commitment, not a treaty requiring ratification. It was arranged in four 'baskets'. The first set out ten principles for relations between states, among them sovereign equality, refraining from force, the inviolability of frontiers, territorial integrity, non-intervention and respect for human rights. The second covered economic, scientific and technical co-operation; the third human contacts, such as family reunification, travel, information and culture; and the fourth follow-up meetings.

At first the Act was widely seen in the West as a gain for Moscow, since it seemed to confirm Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the annexation of the Baltic states, and President Gerald Ford was attacked at home for signing it; the United States insisted that it still did not recognise the annexation, and the text allowed frontiers to change by peaceful means. Over time, however, its human-rights provisions became a tool for dissidents: Helsinki monitoring groups in the Soviet Union and across Europe reported violations, and follow-up meetings in Belgrade, Madrid and Vienna kept up the pressure. The process contributed to the end of the Cold War and was the basis of today's OSCE.

The Soviet Union first sought a European security conference in 1954, hoping for recognition of the post-war borders in Eastern Europe (Office of the Historian).
Détente in the early 1970s led to the Helsinki Consultations of 1972, the opening of the CSCE in July 1973 and negotiations in Geneva from 1973 to 1975 (Office of the Historian).
The Act was not binding and had no treaty status requiring ratification (Wikipedia).
The Act was organised in four baskets.
Basket one listed ten principles including sovereign equality, non-use of force, inviolability of frontiers, territorial integrity, non-intervention and human rights.
Basket two covered economic, scientific and technological co-operation; basket three human contacts, family reunification, travel, information and culture; basket four follow-up.
The Act was seen as a diplomatic gain for the USSR, consolidating post-war borders; Ford faced domestic criticism (Wikipedia).
The US maintained its non-recognition of the Baltic states' incorporation; frontiers could change by peaceful means.
Helsinki monitoring groups tracked violations; follow-up meetings took place in Belgrade (1977-78), Madrid (1980-83) and Vienna (1986-89).
The Helsinki process contributed to the end of the Cold War and was the groundwork for the OSCE.

Q911972.title: Dunkirk evacuation
paras: On 10 May 1940 Germany attacked in the west. While one German army drew the Allies north into Belgium, the main force broke through the French lines at Sedan and drove across northern France to the Channel coast, cutting the Allied armies in two. The British Expeditionary Force (BEF), along with French and Belgian troops, was trapped in a shrinking pocket. After the Germans took Boulogne and Calais, the port of Dunkirk was the only way out.

From 19 May Vice Admiral Bertram Ramsay and his staff, working in the tunnels beneath Dover Castle, were planning an evacuation by sea. On 24 May Hitler halted his tanks short of Dunkirk, partly because his generals feared a counter-attack and Hermann Göring promised that the Luftwaffe could stop any evacuation; the advance resumed on 26 May, but the Allies had gained time. That evening the Royal Navy began Operation Dynamo. Popular accounts say the name came from a room in the Dover tunnels that once held a dynamo, but English Heritage says there is no evidence of this.

The harbour docks were wrecked and the beaches shelved so gently that large ships could not come close, so troops were taken off from the long eastern breakwater (the mole) or ferried out from the beaches in small craft, all under German air attack and shellfire. Progress was slow at first, with only some 7,500 to 8,000 men lifted on the first day, but hundreds of civilian 'little ships', from fishing boats to pleasure craft, answered the navy's call and began arriving from 28 May. Even so, according to English Heritage over two-thirds of the men left from the mole, mostly aboard destroyers and other larger vessels.

British commanders had expected to save about 45,000 men at most. By 4 June, when the last defenders surrendered and the Germans occupied the town, about 338,000 troops had been evacuated, by HISTORY.com's count some 198,000 of them British and 140,000 French. The BEF had abandoned nearly all its heavy equipment, and France surrendered later that month. Churchill warned that 'wars are not won by evacuations', but the rescue of Britain's trained army allowed it to fight on, and 'the miracle of Dunkirk' became a lasting symbol of national resolve.
